utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced, which means that we're ready to start with the examination of your next witness. Mr. Ivetic, that's a witness who has protective measures and is accompanied by representatives of his government. Therefore, the protective measures are face distortion, voice distortion, pseudonym. Therefore, we'll have to go into closed session once the witness enters the courtroom. But I'd first like to have the representatives of his government in the courtroom so that they can be instructed, and we'll, after that, go into closed session to allow the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the representatives of the Canadian government be escorted into the courtroom. Could everyone put on his earphones. Good morning, and welcome in this courtroom. Could you briefly introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLIMAN
utterances.text: Hanya Soliman. I'm with the Department of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soliman.

utterances.speaker: MS. WICKLER
utterances.text: Major Renee Wickler; again from the Department of Defence in Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome to you as well. Before we start, you are here as representatives of your government, and your role is limited. Your role is limited to drawing my attention to any national security concerns that may arise during the examination of the witness, the witness who will testify with pseudonym, face distortion and voice distortion. You should refrain from any direct contact with the witness. If you have any concern, you address me and then, of course, we'll pay proper attention to it. Perhaps after we have moved into private session because the testimony will be given in open session but with the protective measures as announced. If that's clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. WICKLER
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then in order to make the protective measures effective, we'll invite Witness GRM037 - because that's how we will call him - he'll be invited to enter the courtroom once the curtains are down. We briefly move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- is there any way that we could get some. Oh. Thank you, Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, I hereby put on the public record that the witness just has made a solemn declaration in accordance with the Rules, which perhaps I should have invited him to make in open session, but it's hereby on the record. Witness, you'll testify with protective measures. That means face distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym. No one outside this courtroom can see your face, no one will hear your own voice, and you'll be referred to as "Witness GRM037." Please take care yourself as well that in your answers that you never say anything which might reveal your identity. If you think that a truthful answer would put you at such risk, you're invited to address me so that we can move into private session for that portion of your evidence. You'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My colleagues advise me that I should also inform you about the presence of the representatives of the Canadian government. They're here exclusively to draw the attention of this Chamber to any national security concerns they may -- that may arise during your testimony. They're not here to be consulted by you or to give any guidance to you in your role as a witness. If that is clear to you, I'll now invite Mr. Ivetic, and you find him to your left, I invite Mr. Ivetic to start his examination. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, again, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we begin with questions I'd like to remind that you since we will both be speaking in English we need to observe a pause between question and answer to permit the translators and court reporter to do their job. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ivetic, sorry to interrupt again. If you would need at any moment a break, feeling perhaps tired, just address me, and we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The first document we need to look at should not be broadcast to the public. And so the document that should not be broadcast to the public is 65 ter number 1D04139. And again I stress it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could take a moment to look at the on screen and verify for us if your name and birth date are correctly recorded in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D04139 under seal as a confidential exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4139 receives exhibit number D1239, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1239 is admitted under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you have occasion to give a written statement to the Defence team of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please have a look at 1D04140 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recognise this witness statement from the Karadzic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And whose statement is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can please ask that we do not broadcast the next page we go to, I'd like to go to the last page, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is a signature here. Do you recognise whose signature we see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to signing this statement on the date that is written herein, did you have an opportunity to review the same recently to see if any corrections are necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to page 2 and paragraph 10 of the document, and while we're here, I gave a hard copy to the court usher that I believe Prosecution counsel has already looked at. It may assist the witness to have a hard copy in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in paragraph 10, it is written here that you: "Heard" there was a photo showing one of the mortar shells was being detonated by being dropped from a window. Is that accurate that you only heard of this photo or is there a clarification or correction needed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not true. There's a correction or a clarification that is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said I heard, it was a general topic that I had heard that there was and then later on I had seen the photograph, so the correction is not that I just heard it but I also had seen the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, apart from this one clarification to paragraph 10 of your statement from the Karadzic proceedings, do you stand by your written statement as being correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you questions today on the same topics as contained in your written statement, would your answers to me today be the same in substance as is recorded in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth, can we then take your answers as recorded in your written statement to be truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender 1D04140 under seal due to the signature. We do have a public redacted version, 1D04141 which has the signature redacted from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4140 receives exhibit number D1240.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4141 receives exhibit number D1241.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a short summary as per the Rule 92 ter nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please read your summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: GRM037 was an intelligence analyst at UNPROFOR headquarters from November 1994 to July 1995. He later served in UNPROFOR after the Dayton Accords in December 1995. During his time as an intelligence analyst, it was a widely held belief among Western-oriented intelligence analyst, including him, that the Bosnian Muslims were responsible for some of the most notorious shelling incidents in Sarajevo resulting in death and wounding of civilians. It was believed the Muslims shelled their own civilians in order to blame the Serbs and get foreign intervention on their side in the ongoing war. In relation to the first Markale market shelling, a US soldier told the witness the Bosnian Muslims were responsible and showed a photograph of a person dropping a mortar shell from a window overlooking the market. As to the second Markale market shelling, the witness was informed the round was recorded by Cymbeline radar but it could not be determined which side had fired it. A Canadian officer hold the witness about a Turkish C130 aircraft escorted by US F-16 fighter jets which landed. The monitoring organisation had been told to "turn their radars off" on that occasion. As an intelligence analyst, he had credible information that the Bosnian Muslims were violating the weapons exclusion zone in May 1995. Members of UNPROFOR, NATO or national armed forces were tasked with covertly locating targets among the Serbs for NATO air-strikes. Among these were British JCOs and Canadian forward air controllers. Several countries also had their own soldiers working covertly in Bosnia. General Rupert Smith must have known about this. Virtually every UNMO, the witness encountered in Bosnia tried to do sneaking and peeking like James Bond. Many had weapons and were like Rambo, even though they were supposed to be unarmed. The witness believes national elements tasked UNMOs to collect information for them from time to time. The Bosnian Serbs were aware of these activities of the UNMOs. The witness recalls that UNPROFOR headquarters and national contingents, as well as the witness himself, advised UN personnel, including UNMOs, that they may be perceived as combatants by the Bosnian Serbs once NATO air-strikes commenced. And this completes the public summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. I'd like to revisit one matter. You tendered D1241. Now I gave a decision it would be admitted but isn't it true that guidance was that redacted versions of evidence should not be tendered but should be filed and that we have given instruction as to when to file them? I think that's -- so, therefore, I -- we reconsider at this very moment, for technical reasons, up till the moment we have reviewed exactly what our guidance is, D1241 which is now tendered not admitted, or not admitted yet. Or perhaps we could even make it marked for identification now. We would then review exactly what the guidance was and then you are expected to act in accordance with that guidance, which, as far as I remember was filing but at a time as you find in that guidance. This is to avoid that we have matters in evidence which the Chamber -- which do not assist the Chamber but are purely there for the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And, Madam Registrar, the status of D1241 is now changed. MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I do want to ask for some further clarification as to some other parts of your statement. If we can all first look at page 2 and paragraph 9 of the same. And, here, when you say it was a "widely held" belief that Bosnian Muslims were responsible for some of the notorious shelling incidents in Sarajevo, how many such incidents did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There, I am primarily talking about the two marketplace shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And your use of the term "Western-oriented intelligence analysts," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These would be other Western intelligence allies of Canada working for UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what led to you believe that this belief of the culpability of the Bosnian Muslims was widely held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was just a belief that we had from being on the ground and experiencing various other things. It was a belief that the Bosnian Muslims were very adept at winning the public relations war and that they understood the value of these such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 10 where you say that at least -- that it was widely -- it was a widely held belief within the UN forces that at least one of the marketplace shellings was caused by Muslims. At what level within the UN was this belief held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was held at the highest of levels, at the Force Commander level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever personally have occasion to visit Markale market and view the impact imprint of the first Markale market shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know when approximately that would have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I don't recall. It would have been during that first tour though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what were your impressions of the imprint at that occasion during your first tour when you did view it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we looked at the -- I was with one other person. When we looked at the imprint of the shell or the splatter of the round, it looked to be a trajectory of being straight down. It was also such a narrow street that we had anticipated that if it was a fired round it would have had to have been an extremely accurate round to have landed where it did on such a narrow street.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now in both paragraphs 10 and 11 of your statement, you talk of a photograph. And today you have now clarified that you heard and then also saw the photograph in question. What was your understanding of the position from which the photographer had taken that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my understanding that the photographer of the photograph was inside the same room that the person who dropped the mortar shell. They were both in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of the provenance or source that had provided that particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was provided by the Bosnian Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about the rank of the US soldier who showed the photograph or his affiliations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the rank was a US soldier of the rank of a sergeant and he was with the US intelligence cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have a recollection of how close you were personally to the photograph in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say probably about 10 to 15 feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you alone with the US sergeant at the time the photograph was shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were others in the room too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about this photo subsequent to the occasion when it was shown to you and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this meeting or -- pardon me. This occasion when it was shown to you and others, generally speaking, can you tell us what was the function of that gathering. Was it social in nature or official?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was an official meeting. It was a meeting that was designed specifically to talk about that marketplace shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you help us to know approximately what time-frame that meeting took place during, in relation to your deployments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to say that it took place probably in the late November or early December time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, that would be in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Moving along, in paragraph 12, you say for the second shelling of Markale market you were informed that the round had been recorded by Cymbeline radar but then could not be determined from which side of the confrontation line it had been fired from. What is the basis of your knowledge of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a direct conversation that I had with a person who had extensive knowledge of the Cymbeline radar and its use.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when would you have spoken with them about this? And again, if you could tie it with a particular time-period of your deployments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say the second shelling of the Markale marketplace, do you recall the year of that incident, the actual shelling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would not mind, you say you don't remember when you had this discussion or this conversation in which the Cymbeline radar was mentioned. Where did that take place, that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had returned to Canada after my deployment and it was after the -- obviously the incident. It would have been fairly shortly after the incident. I was speaking on a telephone with my counterpart who was still back in -- in -- in the theatre. And I was also speaking with some other foreign nationals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you had a telephone conference then or were these several conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been several conversations, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All by phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let me see if I ... And when you say the second shelling of the Markale marketplace, do you recall the year of the actual shelling that you are referring to as the second marketplace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's in August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall if the UN or NATO undertook any actions as a response to this second marketplace shelling in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's when there was a bombing campaign that started.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who was in charge of operating the Cymbeline radar system in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a joint project between the French and the British.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated you talked with your successor in position on the phone. What were the nationalities of the other individuals that you talked about in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: British.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to move to paragraph 13 of your statement, which we need to scroll down a bit on the screen to see it. Here, you talk about a Turkish C130 aircraft escorted by US F-16s. First of all, can you clarify for us what is the connection between these planes and the title we see just above paragraph 13, that says: "Arms smuggling by air at Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly the connection or the -- was that the Turkish C130 aircraft that was escorted was bringing weapons into the Bosnian Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have knowledge of who controlled Tuzla or -- pardon me. Was there a particular facility or location in Tuzla that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Tuzla air base is what I was referring to, but I do not know exactly because I have not been to Tuzla, that air base I do not know exactly the runway or which runways were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know who would have been in control of Tuzla air base at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, it was under the control of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now apart from this plane at Tuzla, did you have any other knowledge of arms smuggling into the region by way of aeroplane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had personal knowledge of aircraft landing in Zagreb. They would land fairly frequently once probably a week at least land around midnight, unload, and then leave within two or three hours of the morning. On several occasions I personally watched these aircraft land. I could not see what was being unloaded because they would be farther away on the tarmac. On one occasion, which I was not there for, but certainly heard, there was an explosion of one of the aircraft which rocked the entire city of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to focus on paragraph 15, page 3, and here you state that you received "credible information" that the Bosnian Muslims were violating the Sarajevo weapons exclusion zone in May of 1995. What was the nature of this credible information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was probably two. One was the UN situation reports that we received but the other was satellite imagery.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say here it was well-known NATO would not launch air-strikes against Bosnian Muslims because they had support of the US, by whom was this well-known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly discussed at the highest levels within UNPROFOR but also within Canada and its other allies within the UN. We had discussed it frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus on paragraph 16. In paragraph 16, you say that you have personal knowledge that there were personnel on the ground in Bosnia tasked with covertly locating and recording Bosnian Serb positions for NATO air-strikes. What was the basis of your personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basis of my personal knowledge was that I spoke personally to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 18 of your statement on the same page, you say you know national elements were providing information used in compiling the target lists for NATO air-strikes because you saw such lists. Where did you see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was within a cell that was run by the British in the UN UNPROFOR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in paragraph 22, which starts at the bottom of page 3 and continues onto page 4, you say General Rupert Smith must have been aware that forward air controllers on the ground in Bosnia assisted NATO in strikes in May 1995 and that you saw him enter the air operations cell at UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb. Why do you believe that fact is determinative that he must have known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly when he entered the cell from my knowledge of what was happening within that cell, that was certainly the only main operation or the reason for the cell. So for him to enter into the cell, he would be discussing in my mind that type of information and only that type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now here ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- we'll take an early break. There seems to be a little problem with the voice distortion so we'll -- we'll take whatever measure is needed, including an early break. Mr. Ivetic, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Very short. 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen to 20 minutes. We take an early ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take an early break but not until after we've moved into closed session in order to allow the witness to leave the courtroom. We return into closed session, and we'll resume after the break in closed session for the witness to enter the courtroom again. And that will be at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. File, you reported when we were still in closed session that you did not receive audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That problem is resolved. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That problem is resolved. I further put on the record that what I said before the break about the voice distortion that it was a false alarm that turned finally out to be nothing wrong so this is a good message. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we left off talking about paragraph 22 of your statement, the second half of which is visible at the top of page 4 on our monitors at present. Here, you say that you read reports on the work of forward air controllers, special forces, and national elements? Do you know if these reports were shared with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would have been shared with a very small group of countries, certainly within other allies within the -- that Canada would have had within the UN as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this very same paragraph you also mention UN briefings for whom or at what level were these briefings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the morning force commander's briefings at UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to focus on UNMOs which are the main topic of paragraphs 24 through 27 of your statement that we also have on page 4 of your statement. First of all, what category or type of information did you have occasion to receive from UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly I would receive information on weapons emplacements, new fortifications, new weapons coming into the area that UNMO was responsible for, and then general feelings of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, in paragraph 26 of your statement on this same page, you conclude that paragraph talking about UNMOs by saying: "They were like Rambo." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What that means was they were usually -- well, the ones that I dealt with which were from Canada and other countries, were usually armed. They believed that they had the responsibility of doing the intelligence collection of their area, and they were very aggressive in their pursuit of their -- their collecting of information within their area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now for the next questions, Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution, I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could return to your written statement and scroll up just a little bit, I'd like to ask you about paragraph 28. And here in this paragraph, you say that you believe "that UNPROFOR headquarters and national contingents advised their forces in Bosnia that once air-strikes by NATO commenced, they may be perceived by the Bosnian Serbs as combatants." You say: "I recall this being discussed at a morning briefing at UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb which occurred at the Force Commander level, although I do not know if the Force Commander was present on that occasion." For purposes of the advising on the part of UNPROFOR headquarters and the national contingents, what did you understand was the purpose of the same? What was anticipated by them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By UNPROFOR we're speaking specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly it was my understanding that UNPROFOR was well aware that any bombing or any air-strikes would push the Bosnian Serb side to perceive us -- us being the UN at that time - as being combatants within the war. It's something that we talked about extensively within UNPROFOR. I talked about it a lot with the UNPROFOR intelligence cell that was in UNPROFOR and with Canadians as well, talking to Canadians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then the last sentence of this paragraph says: "I also personally advised some UNMOs of this fact." And so now in relation to your advising, I think you may have already answered but what was the purpose or the anticipation behind making such advisements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly just related to keeping specifically Canadian UNMOs and -- safe. And just to -- giving them the heads up, a warning, that they could be perceived as being a combatant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for answering my questions this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. File, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. File. You find Mr. File to your right. Mr. File is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'll give you the same reminder that Mr. Ivetic gave you, which is because we both speak the same language, let's leave a pause between question and answer for the benefit of the interpreters and the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: First I just want to clarify the nature of your prior testimony related to your time in the former Yugoslavia. You testified once before in this Tribunal in the Radovan Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And before you that you gave sworn testimony in a 2005 Canadian Superior Court case called Queen against Nicholas Ribic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If could you kindly answer the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question -- the answer to the question would be that would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And in that case you were known by the pseudonym Witness A; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's your position that in both of those proceedings, the Karadzic case and the Ribic case, you told the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to turn your attention to the shelling of the Markale marketplace in Sarajevo on 5 February 1994 which is Scheduled Incident G8 in this case and is often referred to as Markale I. You arrived in Zagreb approximately nine months after this incident; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And turning your attention to paragraph 11 of your statement as well as your testimony today in your statement you say: "A US soldier told me that the Muslims were responsible for this shelling and displayed what he said was a photograph of a person dropping a mortar shell from a window overlooking the Markale marketplace. I did not examine this photograph." Now, on direct examination you confirmed that you saw this photograph from a distance of about 10 to 15 feet; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And the size of the photograph appeared to you to be of a traditional snap-shot size; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So in inches or centimetres, whichever you prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5 by 8, I guess, I do believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Inches or centimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. That would be inches.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The US soldier flashed it very quickly and then put it away again; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And he did not hold it still and you could not see what was on the picture; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But you were led to believe by comments from this US sergeant that it depicted the interior of a room with someone holding a mortar shell; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the US sergeant in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: On direct, you said that this happened during a meeting the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb. Who was the most senior UNPROFOR official who was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would have been one other person probably of a bit higher rank of myself at that time. I was a sergeant at the time. There was a British person also that was there with me. I do believe he was a higher rank, properly a warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But you can't remember this person's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You spent the first eight years of your military career in an artillery corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Did you have any experience handling mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So you must have understood that mortar shell versus a variety of safety features that are intended to avoid an accidental explosion caused by the crew that is handling the shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that there are certainly mortar shells -- most mortar shells do have precautions and that they need to be spinning in order to activate the fuse. But there are to my knowledge, there are some that do not require any of the spinning motion and are simply a point detonating fuse, that if they hit something or if a hammer was to hit them, they would go off.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So you are aware that one of the safety features of a mortar shell is located in the mortar shell's fuse itself, which is that it will not be armed unless it undergoes the massive acceleration of being fired out of a mortar tube?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm obviously not making myself clear. Yes, most mortar shells, I understand, have to have that acceleration to arm the fuse, but there are some mortar shells that are produced that either the fuse can be tampered with so it becomes point detonating, and it does not need to spin. Any kind of detonation or hitting of that fuse will set it off. And there are some mortar shells that are designed that way and do not need to spin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can you give an example of a mortar shell that would just explode any time it was dropped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was my understanding and explained to me that the mortar shell in question on the marketplace, the ones that were designed and supplied by Russians or manufactured by Russians, were the ones that were point detonating and did not need to be armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm asking about your knowledge of a model of a mortar shell that is always armed that can explode whenever it's dropped even if it is being handled by a mortar crew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking if I know of that as true? Yes, I believe that to be true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But you can't give me a model number of any artillery that does that, any mortar that does that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I certainly cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would seek one clarification. In your previous answer you said in -- the mortar shell in question on the marketplace that there were supplied or manufactured by the Russians. Did they tell you that this shell was supplied by the Russians or manufactured by Russians? Is that what they told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was my understanding that the 120-millimetre mortar shells that were being used in the theatre were Russian-manufactured ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking in general. Was there any specific about this mortar shell being of a type produced, manufactured by the Russians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what was discussed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Discussed? I mean, were you told that this specifically was such a Russian-manufactured projectile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This specific one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This specific one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your previous answer, you were rather talking general terms, that is, mortar shells used were of Russian origin, which is a bit of a different approach compared to, They told me that this projectile, this mortar shell was a Russian-manufactured one. Now, which of the two was it, that specific explanation given to you, or was it your general understanding of the type of shells that were used in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I was told specifically that the mortar that was used or the mortars that were used at the marketplace shelling were Russian designed and manufactured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you have no personal knowledge whether that's true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a follow-up. Who told you this, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was discussed when I was in the room with the Americans and the British.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who told me? It was an American, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The American, sir, who was holding the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know his name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I know his name? No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- one second, please. Yes, did you report this information anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it was a Russian shell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That the photograph was shown to you where it was told that this was a person in a room who would throw, shell a mortar shell from a window.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not discussed with UNPROFOR but I would have sent it back to Canada in a situation report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have reported in a situation report that you were told that a photograph was shown to you, although at a distance, where it was explained to you that this was the -- a person throwing a mortar shell on the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Though, needless to say, of course, that if there's any documentary support for this, of course, the Chamber would very much like to receive that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And just to clarify, you haven't provided that -- a copy of any report that you drafted to anyone related to this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You testified at transcript -- temporary transcript page 12 that you were told the photo was "provided by the Bosnian Muslim side." So your understanding was that Bosnian Muslims provided UNPROFOR with documentation of their own conspiracy, and you just accepted that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a small clarification. Not UNPROFOR but provided the US.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But that didn't change the conclusion that you still accepted that that was the case when you were told this; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You also testified about visiting the location of this shelling at temporary transcript pages 11 to 12. And just to clarify, you said you didn't know when you visited the location but it was sometime during your first tour. So that's between November 1994 and July 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you said you visited this location with one other person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, I just remember it was my British counterpart that was working with the British forces but I do not know his name, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: At transcript page 12, you described the location as being on a "narrow street." But you're aware that the Markale I incident happened in a market square, not a street; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You were not given the task by your superiors to go to the scene of this incident many months after it took place to try to determine who was responsible; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. It was not tasked, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you did not consult any of the reports drafted by the on-site investigation teams; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You did not look at any of the photographic or video evidence from the scene immediately after the explosion; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You were not aware of how the tail-fin of 120-millimetre mortar had lodged in the pavement or the angle of entry it revealed; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You never, in the course of your career, served as part of a team that conducted forensic examinations of mortar craters in order to determine the origin of fire of a specific mortar round; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to switch topics now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter number 33154. This may be listed as "under seal," but I believe it is not necessary to have it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is a copy of your testimony from the Ribic case that we were talking about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we go to e-court page 64, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So before I ask about this, the content, the format of this is the two of the lawyers in the case reading testimony that you had previously given out of the presence of the jury; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So when you see answers from Mr. DePoe he's reading your sworn testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So directing your attention to the bottom half of the page you were asked the question: "Is it true that the orders to take hostages came from the top level of the Serb leadership? " The answer was: "I received this intelligence information from direct sources. "So this is done at a very high level. This is not a local commander in the field gets to make the decision to take hostages. "Certainly within the Serbian army and the Muslim" - and we're now on the next page in e-court: "...and Croat for that matter, it's the old Soviet style or old Communist style of mentality that a person doesn't make a decision, a soldier doesn't make a decision unless it comes from higher up. You want that authority because, not like Canada, if you make a mistake, you may get charged and then have you a court-martial. Here you get shot. Even the battalion commanders are going to be very careful about what they do because they'll get shot if they make the wrong decision. "So, these type of things would be very high up." Do you recall giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific but I recall generally that that would be my impression, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And when you said "very high up," you were talking about very high up in the military structure; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 of your statement, you indicate that you were present in the former Yugoslavia in May 1995 when the NATO air-strikes were carried out in Pale, but you personally were not in Pale at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So any information that you have about what was going on on the ground in Pale, you had received second-hand. You didn't observe it yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And the information that you received about the hostage crisis was delayed by hours or even a day; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm understanding exactly the question. I don't -- it would be hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case, at transcript page 32033, you were shown a copy of your testimony from the Ribic case, where you said: "It's within maybe hours or a day or whatever, but it's not minute by minute." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. But I do believe that it is probably something I would have said and I'm trying to say the same thing right now, that it was within hours, not minute by minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I want to also ask you about some of the general comments you make about UNMOs in your statement, especially paragraphs 24 to 27. The basis for your opinions here comes from your interaction with them as sources of information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And in your statement at paragraph 26, you also discussed this today at temporary transcript 21, you say: "Although UNMOs were supposed to be unarmed, many of them had weapons. They were like Rambo." Now from your answer today, when you talked about them being armed and aggressive what you meant by this is that they looked and acted like Rambo; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You're talking about the film character Rambo; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You would admit that is an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You are aware that engaging in this kind of exaggeration could have the effect of demeaning your United Nations colleagues from that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I have a minute to think about that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A lot of the question is lost in the transcript at this moment. I know that it will be worked over this evening, but perhaps you could read it again not to ask the witness to answer it again but at least we have it also written form before us if we want to further consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The question was: You are aware that engaging in this kind of exaggeration could have the effect of demeaning your United Nations colleagues from that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that was the question the witness has answered. It may also have reminded you, Mr. File, that speaking more slowly gives certainly a good transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you for the reminder, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, none of the UNMOs that you claimed were armed were part of the group that was taken hostage in May 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now also in your statement at paragraphs 16 to 22, you talk about the presence of forward air controllers in Bosnia. To your knowledge, no one in the group that was taken hostage in May 1995 was one of these forward air controllers; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That last question, could I have you say it once more? Just because I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- if -- do you have a transcript on your screen before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you can re-read it paragraph [sic] 37, line 3, where starts now also in your statement, so you could re-read that question. Therefore, page 37, line 3. And if there's anything you'd like to add, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I can see the question. When you talk about the forward air controllers in the group that was taken hostage, which group are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm actually just going to refer you to your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter number 33152. This will be e-court page 14. If we could go to page 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You can see at the bottom of that page, actually. It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we go back to the previous page. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: At the last line of the page, you were asked: "Were any of the hostages who were taken into custody in May 1995 some of ..." -- And then we can go to the next page: "... these forward air controllers of which you speak? " And your answer is: "No, not that I'm aware of." That was your testimony from the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch off your microphone, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. File. I would have a few more questions, but I need a little bit of time to prepare myself for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you have seen that photograph. You were told that this was someone who was at a window overlooking the Markale market with a mortar shell. Could I, first of all, ask you, what were you able to verify from that distance? Could you confirm that this was what was depicted on that photograph, or did you say it was at such a distance I couldn't see it but you just accepted that the description was accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was strictly waved in front and then put back down. I had -- did not have an opportunity to see anything whatsoever on the picture itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you thought this to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly believed what the person was telling me was -- because the discussion was based on -- on -- on that marketplace shelling. So I certainly believed it to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you given it some thought on - apart from the technicalities of the mortar shells - whether it would be likely that someone would throw a mortar shell from a window and that mortar shell then to end at the place where the shell exploded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've given it a lot of thought, the photograph, and the actual dropping of the mortar shell. If you're asking do I honestly believe that they dropped a mortar shell? Am I understanding is that the question you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's what was suggested to you and indeed, that you think about whether this was likely to have happened and if you would call that belief, then I would not contradict you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, it is something I would believe would have been -- would have occurred or could have occurred at that time in Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, my question is not whether that could have occurred in Bosnia, to throw a shell from a window, but whether it was likely that someone would have thrown a shell from one of the surrounding buildings on the Markale market and for it then to detonate at the place where it did so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do think that it is likely that that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of what weighs a mortar shell approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 120-millimetre mortar shell, I would -- I would be just guessing, because I have handled mortar shells of that size. They are very heavy. They have to be in the 50-pound range, 30, 40, 50-pound range. But that would be a guess, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you consider that the distance between the place where the shell exploded and the building from which it would have been thrown was such that you could just by throwing put a -- well, let's just assume a 50-pound shell over that distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is actually probably the thing that cemented the most in my mind that it is possible. Looking at where the shell impacted, it's not a long ways away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long is it approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three feet from where the building is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean the small market building or do you mean one of the surrounding buildings where people may have worked and lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember and recall, directly behind where the shell impacted. The building right behind it. It's only about three feet from the building, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what is behind the impact depends on where you stand. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you change your position then, of course, what is behind the shell is another feature comparing to where you were a second ago. Could you tell us, you said 3 metres from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3 feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3 feet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you now thinking in terms of three feet from a high-rise building several floors or are you talking about a lower construction which would have been the market building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was from my recollection it was a three-storey or so building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have P868, page 50. I was unable to verify whether I had the right page on my e-court because it didn't function well, but I hope that ... Could we move ... let me see. One second, please. If you just allow me one second so as to prepare myself for my follow-up questions. I'm having ... I have technical problems with my own e-court. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some technical difficulties, but let's move on. Let's take the next page in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise, but I haven't overcome my technical problems. I still need a bit of time but one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do note that we are almost at the time for the break. I don't know if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is once I leave the courtroom I don't have access to my e-court any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go to page 52 in e-court. Witness, this is a view of the Markale market. Just forget about any arrows. Could you tell us what type of building you said the shell fell at a distance of 1 metre, well, 3 feet of? Perhaps you see it best on the left-hand picture which is a photograph rather than a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm looking at that, but I'm still confused on both pictures as to where the actual road is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm inviting the parties to agree on it, but as far as my recollection assists me, what is seen just in the very front of this photograph is the -- is a car, which is on the road, which passes by the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, that's our understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I believe there's a rail that separates the pedestrian walkway that we see just above the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you see therefore the street is just in the front part of the photograph? We see some stalls on the market. Could you give us an indication as to where you think that shell fell at 3 feet from a multi-storey building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but could you have somebody indicate to me where the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall -- this picture does not in my mind -- make me remember what I saw whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then bear a second with me. Could we go to page 13 in this same document. Before I put a question to you, do the parties agree that what is depicted here, right or wrong, is -- at least the dark dot, is where the one who drew this sketch locates the impact?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Without knowing how this diagram was made, no Your Honours, I would suggest page 55 of the document which is a photograph of the actual place where the projectile fell. That might be better than a drawing prepared by an unknown person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is what we understand it to be. It is showing the relationship between the location of the impact and the location that the individual mentioned at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Ivetic, you thought it would be better to have a look at page 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's look at page 55 in the original and then we may go back to 13. Could we enlarge a bit the middle part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm putting to you - and please respond - if this is the place of impact and it is in a sketch - and you see that on your screen as well, I think - is depicted, right or wrong, that there's no way that the point of impact would be been 3 feet of a building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that all your thoughts about how likely there would have been to throw a mortar shell with your hands reaching this place is that your thoughts were, rather, on loose grounds if the distance is, indeed, totally different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am at a loss. I do not recognise the picture. You showed a picture before of a building right beside a tall building. So.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are -- I'm asking you now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not to again start thinking about the matter but to either confirm or deny with proper reasons that what you see here, that this point of impact is not within 3 feet of any building, irrespective of what building we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that is the impact I would absolutely agree with Your Honour, yes, it's not within 3 feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you have told us that you have been on that market and you could have known unless you say this you say this is not what you saw as an impact on the ground of the market.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you at that time -- were you able -- because that was at the basis of your thoughts that this was within 3 feet of a building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basis of my thoughts were, yes, because it was within 3 feet of a high-rise building it was able to be dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But looking at this, is that still your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Yes, we'll first take a break. That's -- I'm reminded by my colleagues that it's time for the break. But before we take the break, we first move into closed session so as to allow the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, during cross-examination, you were asked about the photograph that was shown to you and you said that it was flashed and then put away and then at temporary transcript page 39 in answering questions of the Judges you said there was a discussion as to the Markale market shelling during the course of that meeting. The first question I want to ask you is did that discussion into the shelling -- the first shelling of Markale marketplace take place before or after the photograph was flashed to yourself and others in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been immediately right after.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have any approximation as to how long that discussion lasted, talking about the Markale marketplace shelling after that photograph had been flashed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fifteen, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you identified or mentioned a sitrep that you would have sent back to Canada about this. Do you recall what security classification level such sitreps would have been marked with at the time they were sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one was -- when I said a sitrep, it was a phone call that I had made. I recall calling back to Canada and discussing the incident. It would have been -- as far as classification it would have been secret and it probably would have been Canadian eyes only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it have been Canadian ears not eyes because it was a telephone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me, sir? I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said it was a telephone call. It was not a written document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was a telephone call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it would have been for Canadian ears, not eyes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want to thank you for answering my questions and for coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness. We do have one matter that we need to discuss before the guests from Canada leave the courtroom. As far as I'm concerned we could excused the witness but we would want to jointly address you on another matter following the witness's departure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would have a question for the witness. Twice you mentioned counterparts today. The first time you said you were back in Canada but you were "speaking on a telephone with my counterpart who was still back in the theatre." Who was that counterpart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I do not recall the name of the person who replaced me in theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was a Canadian intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The second time you mentioned a counterpart was, and I quote from page 32, line 12: "Once again, I just remember it was my British counterpart that was working with the British forces but I do not know his name." How long did you work together with this British counterpart of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably about three or four months of my tour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you don't know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am afraid not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know any names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like take you back to this photograph. Was it a colour photograph or a black-and-white photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, black and white, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did anybody look at this photograph during that discussion which followed the showing of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was it who had this photograph in his hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The United States sergeant that was part of the intelligence cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I would like to take you back to paragraph 28 of your statement. There you say, I quote: "I believe that UNPROFOR headquarters and national contingents advised their forces in Bosnia that once air-strikes by NATO commenced, they may be perceived as Bosnian Serbs -- by the Bosnian Serbs as combatants." Who are those you are referring to in this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't see the word "those" in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "I believe that UNPROFOR headquarters and national contingents advised their forces." Who are these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their forces, you're talking about UNPROFOR, their forces? That would be in headquarters, any of the UNPROFOR nations that were involved in the UNPROFOR headquarters, it was discussed that there would be -- it would be possible seeing the UN as being one-sided and being combatants. So what I'm referring to there is anyone who was sitting in that UNPROFOR meeting at that time, because the UNPROFOR meetings were open to all UNPROFOR countries they were allowed to have people at that meeting, any of these people would have gone back to their own national people, their contingents in theatre and explained it to them that they may be seen as combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was heading this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What was the function of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not recall either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which -- which nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a British intelligence that was also giving a briefing and it may have came from him. He was -- and I do not recall his name whatsoever. But it was at the commander's level of briefing that was done every morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you remember any name of any of the participants of that meeting? If you are hesitant to mention the name in public session you may ask for moving into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I speak with the Canadian representatives first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're supposed not to speak to them but apparently the representatives of the government have not expressed any concerns. It was offered to you to give the name in private session. If I do not hear of any objections to that solution, if we would follow that course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLIMAN
utterances.text: We're fine with going in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you attend this meeting, sir, of -- that you referred to in paragraph 28? Where this matter was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you assumed that your Canadian colleague attended. You are not recollecting that you saw him there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm recollecting that we spoke around that time-frame, but I don't know whether -- he was a briefer for -- for that UNPROFOR meeting, and I don't recall -- there was -- because there was four or five briefers, whether he was at that meeting or not. At the first one. But he certainly would have had the same type of -- of thought process that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But you said you assume he attended the meeting. Surely you would have seen him if he had attended the meeting if you were also there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because he would probably have been briefing. But I don't recall whether it was him that gave the actual briefing or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you mentioned with respect to the photograph that the person who was briefing you about it sort of flashed it and put it down. It was something like an 8 by 5 inches photograph, according to your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm saying 8 by 5 but I'm talking about a normal photograph, a snapshot. It wasn't a blown-up version or anything. I'm just saying 8 by 5 and I'm just doing that by quick arithmetic in my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this was at 15 feet distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
